claims.text: Dynamic behavior in solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is governed by a transition in the dominant plasticity mechanism across temperature and strain-rate regimes.
Thermally activated dislocation glide dominates deformation at high temperatures and low strain rates.
Nano-twinning or shear-transformation-zone-mediated deformation dominates at low temperatures and high strain rates.
Variations in effective stacking-fault energy and local lattice distortions drive the proposed transition in plasticity mechanism.
As-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn has a typical polycrystalline microstructure.
As-cast Co-free FeNiCrMn contains inherent local lattice distortions.
Effective stacking-fault energy and local lattice distortions mediate the relative ease of dislocation motion, twin nucleation, and shear transformation.
Thermal activation at elevated temperature eases dislocation motion.
Elevated-temperature, low-strain-rate dislocation glide produces moderate strain hardening.
Low temperature and high strain rate increase the barrier to dislocation motion.
An increased barrier to dislocation motion shifts deformation toward nano-twinning or localized shear events.
Nano-twinning or localized shear events enhance short-term ductility and strain hardening.
High-temperature, low-strain-rate deformation will exhibit primarily dislocation motion and lower strain hardening.
Low-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation will exhibit increased twin or shear-transformation activity and higher strain hardening.
The low-temperature, high-strain-rate mechanism will maintain the alloy's strength–ductility balance.
At moderate temperature and strain rate, a balance of dislocation glide and limited twin formation defines mechanical behavior.
Significant post-solidification annealing or defect evolution may alter the proposed microstructural mediators and invalidate the mechanism.
Simulation scale and limitations of interatomic potentials can affect the fidelity of the predicted deformation mechanism.
